lessonRef.subject: mathematics
lessonRef.focus: estimating a population mean and margin of error by simulation
lessonRef.title: Concept model B: estimating a population mean and margin of error by simulation

sections.title: Instructional examples
sections.directions: Compare these two examples. Find the step where they stop being the same.

items.prompt: Mean 100, sd 15. What percentage lies between 70 and 130?

steps: That is 100 ± 30, which is two standard deviations.

items.prompt: What does a randomised experiment support?

sections.title: Guided practice
sections.directions: Work these with your teaching parent. Say the reason for each step out loud before you write it.

items.prompt: A random sample of 2500 people gives a sample proportion of 45%. Using the conservative margin of error 1/√n, give the approximate margin of error and the resulting interval.
In 100 simulations under the assumption of no difference, 4 produced a result at least as extreme as the one observed. What should be concluded?
choices: The simulation proves that the observed difference is real.
The simulation proves that there is no difference.
The observed result is statistically significant: it occurred in only 4% of simulations, below the usual 5% threshold.
The observed result is not statistically significant: it occurred in 4% of simulations, which is not unusual.

items.prompt: A quantity is approximately normal with mean 83 and standard deviation 3. Approximately what percentage of values lie between 74 and 92?

sections.title: Independent practice
sections.directions: Work on your own. Show the steps that produced each answer.

items.prompt: A researcher runs a sample survey with randomly selected participants. What kind of conclusion does this design support?
choices: It supports both generalisation and causation, provided the sample is large.
It supports generalising from the sample to the population, but not a causal claim.
It supports a causal conclusion about the treatment, within the population studied.
It supports neither generalisation nor causation, because self-selection can bias both.

items.prompt: A random sample of 625 people gives a sample proportion of 73%. Using the conservative margin of error 1/√n, give the approximate margin of error and the resulting interval.
In 100 simulations under the assumption of no difference, 1 produced a result at least as extreme as the one observed. What should be concluded?
choices: The observed result is statistically significant: it occurred in only 1% of simulations, below the usual 5% threshold.
The simulation proves that there is no difference.
The observed result is not statistically significant: it occurred in 1% of simulations, which is not unusual.
The simulation proves that the observed difference is real.

items.prompt: A quantity is approximately normal with mean 50 and standard deviation 20. Approximately what percentage of values lie between 10 and 90?

sections.title: Mastery check
sections.directions: Mastery check. Work without help, then stop and hand this section in.

items.prompt: A researcher runs an observational study of volunteers who chose their own group. What kind of conclusion does this design support?
choices: It supports both generalisation and causation, provided the sample is large.
It supports a causal conclusion about the treatment, within the population studied.
It supports generalising from the sample to the population, but not a causal claim.
It supports neither generalisation nor causation, because self-selection can bias both.
